title: KV hit elasticity, key curation, TTL governance runbook and safe apply
creator: Aisha Verma
description: Objective: Produce an operational runbook and automated tooling for KV/prefix cache configuration that optimizes cost via hit-rate-aware TTLs and curated cache keys while minimizing customer-visible regressions through staged apply and deterministic rollback. Background: We observe large variance in per-prefix hit elasticity (hit rate sensitivity to TTL and batching) across workloads (chat, embeddings, reranking). Existing autotuners have reduced cost but occasionally cause tail-latency or quality regressions when aggressive TTLs evict useful prefixes during bursts. This ticket synthesizes hit-elasticity modeling, key curation heuristics, governance thresholds, and a safety-first apply/rollback orchestration for runtime and Dedicated deployments.
acceptance_criteria: A1: Deliver a runbook describing hit-elasticity profiling, key curation rules, and TTL governance thresholds with examples for three workload archetypes (chat-short, chat-long, embeddings).
A2: Implement a canary apply workflow that stages TTL changes to 5% traffic, evaluates predefined safety metrics for 72 hours, and either promotes or auto-rolls back based on thresholds.

A3: Provide a telemetry dashboard (cost delta, per-prefix hit-rate, request egress, 95/99 latencies, model token cost) and a cost forecast model showing expected monthly savings and worst-case risk scenarios.
A4: Publish a small CLI helper and JSON schema for recommended key-curation rules and TTL presets; documentation and runbook reviewed by PM and SRE and marked Approved.
A5: No customer-facing incidents within 30 days of rollout for canary-promoted policies (if incident occurs, root cause and improved guard added to runbook).
implementation_plan: 1) Profiling: run a 14-day trace replay with stratified sampling across customer cohorts to estimate per-prefix hit elasticity (Δhit / ΔTTL) and peak-quantile exposure. Use offline simulator to compute cost and tail-latency trade-offs for TTL sweeps. 2) Key curation: produce a taxonomy that groups prefixes into stable/mutable/ephemeral buckets. Rules: prefer natural canonicalization (strip session ids, timestamps), aggregate low-cardinality affixes, and mark high-entropy prefixes for short TTLs. 3) TTL governance: define guardrails — default conservative TTLs, escalation thresholds, and elasticity tiers (Low, Medium, High). Map tiers to rollout speed and canary fraction. 4) Canary tooling: implement a controller that applies TTL deltas via staged rollout (1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%), collects safety metrics and enforces automatic rollback when any metric crosses a fail threshold. 5) Safety signals & thresholds: hit-rate regression > 10% absolute for core prefixes; 95th token latency increase > 20%; token-cost increase > 5% for promoted variants; error-rate spikes; SLO burn rate anomaly. 6) Human-in-the-loop: require PM or SRE approval before promoting to 100% if cost savings > 30% or if any high-risk prefixes were changed. 7) Observability: add dashboard panels and alerts for the canary, and enable shadow replays for 24h after promotion. 8) Docs & training: publish runbook, example configs, and a postmortem template. 9) Rollout: pilot on non-enterprise tenants for 2 weeks, then opt-in for larger customers. 10) Post-deploy: run a 30-day evaluation and lock in recommended presets in the Optimize suggestions UI.
notes_and_risks: Risks: over-aggressive TTL can increase model token cost if cache churn pushes more traffic to model backends; shard hot-spotting if key-canonicalization concentrates traffic; regressions in bursty workloads where ephemeral prefixes suddenly become hot. Mitigations: conservative default presets, elasticity-aware promotion schedule, and automatic rollback triggers. Operational cost: needs additional sampling budget and replay infra to safely estimate elasticity.
